worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $14,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,$ $\pm 2,$ $\pm 7$ and $\pm 14.$

- The leading coefficient is $12,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,$ $\pm 2,$ $\pm 3,$ $\pm 4,$ $\pm 6$ and $\pm 12.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{3}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{1}{6}, & \pm \frac{1}{12}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{2}, & \pm \frac{2}{3}, & \pm \frac{2}{4}, & \pm \frac{2}{6}, & \pm \frac{2}{12}, \\ \pm \frac{7}{1}, & \pm \frac{7}{2}, & \pm \frac{7}{3}, & \pm \frac{7}{4}, & \pm \frac{7}{6}, & \pm \frac{7}{12}, \\ \pm \frac{14}{1}, & \pm \frac{14}{2}, & \pm \frac{14}{3}, & \pm \frac{14}{4}, & \pm \frac{14}{6}, & \pm \frac{14}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to the lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{3}, & \pm \frac{1}{4}, & \pm \frac{1}{6}, & \pm \frac{1}{12}, \\ \pm 2, & \pm 1, & \pm \frac{2}{3}, & \pm \frac{1}{2}, & \pm \frac{1}{3}, & \pm \frac{1}{6}, \\ \pm 7, & \pm \frac{7}{2}, & \pm \frac{7}{3}, & \pm \frac{7}{4}, & \pm \frac{7}{6}, & \pm \frac{7}{12}, \\ \pm 14, & \pm 7, & \pm \frac{14}{3}, & \pm \frac{7}{2}, & \pm \frac{7}{3}, & \pm \frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that several potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates, and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{12},\,\pm \frac{1}{6},\,\pm \frac{1}{4},\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{1}{2},\,\pm \frac{7}{12},\,\pm \frac{2}{3},\,\pm 1,\,\pm \frac{7}{6},\,\pm \frac{7}{4},\,\pm 2,\,\pm \frac{7}{3},\,\pm \frac{7}{2},\,\pm \frac{14}{3},\,\pm 7,\,\pm 14.
$$

This makes a total of $32$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm $ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2\cdot 16=32.$)

Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form ±factor of the constant termfactor of the leading coefficient.

For the given polynomial:

  • The constant term is 14, and its factors are ±1, ±2, ±7 and ±14.

  • The leading coefficient is 12, and its factors are ±1, ±2, ±3, ±4, ±6 and ±12.

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator: ±11,±12,±13,±14,±16,±112,±21,±22,±23,±24,±26,±212,±71,±72,±73,±74,±76,±712,±141,±142,±143,±144,±146,±1412.

Next, we reduce the fractions to the lowest terms: ±1,±12,±13,±14,±16,±112,±2,±1,±23,±12,±13,±16,±7,±72,±73,±74,±76,±712,±14,±7,±143,±72,±73,±76.

Notice that several potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates, and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have ±112,±16,±14,±13,±12,±712,±23,±1,±76,±74,±2,±73,±72,±143,±7,±14.

This makes a total of 32 potential roots. (Remember that each ± sign accounts for 2 roots, and 2⋅16=32.)
